Palliative

/PAL-ee-uh-tiv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Palliative means relieving pain or a problem's symptoms without addressing the underlying cause.

The free desserts were palliative, sweetening the diners' mood without doing anything about the kitchen's hour-long waits.

Worked Example

When employees complained about mandatory weekend shifts, management's response was to install a foosball table in the break room. The staff immediately recognized the gesture as palliative.

The foosball table is meant to make people feel a little better, but the actual problem, the weekend shifts, is left completely untouched. That is exactly what palliative describes: easing the discomfort of a problem without curing its cause.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

comforting: Comforting means giving ease and reassurance — a comforting word, a comforting presence. It works on feelings and can come from anyone. Palliative is a more clinical judgment: a palliative measure targets the symptoms of a problem it cannot cure, easing the pain while the cause stays untouched.

stopgap: A stopgap is a temporary fix used until a real solution is found — the key is that a better answer is expected. Palliative implies no such wait: a palliative treatment eases pain or symptoms when the cause cannot be fixed at all, or is simply being left unfixed.

mitigating: Mitigating means making a harm less severe, and it attaches to risks, damage, and circumstances of every kind — mitigating measures, mitigating factors. Palliative is narrower and clinical: it eases the symptoms of a problem while the underlying cause goes untreated, as palliative care does.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

curative: actually curing the underlying disease or problem

corrective: fixing the root cause of a fault

Where it sits · how deep into the illness it reaches — soothing → palliative → curative

soothing vs. palliative: Soothing is weaker than palliative — a soothing cup of tea gives mild, surface comfort, while a palliative treatment deliberately targets real symptoms it cannot cure.

curative vs. palliative: Curative is stronger than palliative, a palliative medicine eases the pain of an illness, while a curative one eliminates the illness itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — palli

Root — palli: cloak, covering (from Latin pallium, a cloak)

Suffix — -ative

Suffix — -ative: tending to, serving to

Put it together

Put it together: Palliative literally means tending to cloak. A palliative measure throws a cloak over a problem, covering up the pain or discomfort while leaving whatever causes it untouched underneath.

Use the root in a new word: palliate

Use the root in a new word: palliate: City officials tried to palliate residents' frustration with a round of public apologies, though the water shortages continued unchanged.

Word Building

Word Choice

Formal / medical

Most common in medical and policy contexts, as in palliative care or a palliative measure. Do not confuse palliative with preventive: a preventive step stops a problem from ever starting, while a palliative one only eases a problem that already exists.
